title: The Daily Reflection Tree
description: A deterministic end-of-day reflection tool walking employees through three psychological axes: Locus of Control (Axis 1), Contribution vs Entitlement (Axis 2), and Radius of Concern (Axis 3).

axis1.internal: You held the wheel today — even when the road got rough. That's a practiced habit.
axis1.external: Today's weight pulled your attention outward. Somewhere in there, a choice was still yours.
axis1.mixed: You moved between agency and reaction today. Which moments felt most like you?

axis2.contribution: You gave more than you tracked. That's the kind of work that holds things together.
axis2.entitlement: You were paying close attention to the ledger — what was owed and what was fair.
axis2.mixed: You gave some and kept score some. When you gave without tracking — how did that feel?

axis3.altro: Your lens was wide today — others were in the frame, not just you.
axis3.self: Today was mostly yours to carry. Who else was quietly changed by how your day went?
axis3.mixed: You moved between self and others. When you were most zoomed out — what did it feel like?

nodes.text:
Good evening. You made it through the day.

This is a short reflection — not a performance review, not a survey. Just a structured conversation with yourself.

Answer honestly. There are no right answers. It takes about ten minutes.
Let's start simply. As you sit with today — which one word fits it best?

options.label: Rewarding
Productive
Challenging
Draining

nodes.comment: Route based on opening word — positive words to agency-high path, negative to agency-low path

nodes.text: You described today as '{A1_OPEN.answer}'. When things went well, what was the main reason?

options.label: I made deliberate choices that paid off
I adapted in the moment when things didn't go to plan
My team came through — I leaned on them and they delivered
Things aligned — I happened to be in the right place

nodes.text: You described today as '{A1_OPEN.answer}'. When things got hard, where did your mind go first?

options.label: To what I could still control — and I focused there
To who or what caused the problem
To what I could learn from it, even while it was happening
To how unfair or avoidable the situation was

nodes.comment: Route to deeper Axis 1 question based on signal accumulated from Q2

nodes.text: When you held your ground today — what did that actually look like in practice?

options.label: I paused before reacting and chose my response deliberately
I stayed focused on what I could move and let the rest go
I pushed through even when I was doubting myself
Honestly — I'm not sure it was a conscious choice. It just happened.

nodes.text: Looking back at the hardest moment today — was there anything, even small, that was still yours to decide?

options.label: Yes — I could have responded differently, and I can see that now
Maybe — but the situation really did constrain my options
Not really — I was reacting to what others had already set in motion
There was one thing I chose, even if everything else felt out of my hands

nodes.comment: Route to Axis 1 reflection based on final accumulated signals

nodes.text:
You held the wheel today — even when the road got rough.

That's not confidence. It's a practiced habit: noticing where your hand still rests on the controls, even when the engine feels like it's out of reach.

That habit compounds.

Today's weight pulled your attention outward — to what caused the problem, to who should have acted differently, to circumstances that genuinely constrained you. Some of that was accurate.

But somewhere in there, a choice was still yours. Not to assign blame. Just to find it — so it's available to you next time.

You moved between agency and reaction today. Sometimes you found the wheel; sometimes the situation did the driving.

That's honest — most days are mixed. The question worth carrying: which moments felt most like you?

You've looked at how you moved through what today gave you.

Now let's look at something different: not how you responded — but what you brought. Your orientation.
Think about the energy you brought to work today. Which of these fits best?

options.label: I was focused on what I could give and contribute
I felt I deserved more recognition than I got
I showed up, did my work, and helped where I could
I was tracking whether others were pulling their weight

nodes.comment: Route based on axis2 signal accumulated from A2_OPEN

nodes.text: You came in with something to give. Where did most of your energy actually go today?

options.label: Into a problem nobody else seemed to be picking up
Into helping someone who was stuck
Into doing my own work well, even when it went unnoticed
Into worrying whether my effort was being fairly measured

nodes.text: You noticed what felt unfair or unrecognized today. What would 'fair' have actually looked like?

options.label: A word of recognition — something to show my work was seen
Others matching the effort I was putting in
Fewer obstacles placed in front of work that matters
Honestly — maybe just finding something worth giving regardless

nodes.comment: Route to Axis 2 reflection based on accumulated signals

nodes.text:
Today, your energy moved outward. You gave something — attention, effort, care — without needing to balance the ledger.

That's not selflessness. It's the kind of work that holds things together. Teams run on it. Most people don't notice it until it stops.

You were paying close attention to the ledger today — to what felt owed, unacknowledged, or unevenly distributed. That sensitivity isn't wrong; sometimes it's accurate.

But here's the question worth sitting with: when the ledger was running, were you still fully in the room?

You gave some and kept score some. That's ordinary — most people do both.

The interesting question isn't the ratio. It's: when you gave without tracking, how did that feel compared to when you were counting?

You've looked at how you responded today, and what you brought to it.

One last lens. The size of the frame — who else was in the room with you today, even if you didn't notice them at the time.
When you think about today's biggest challenge — whose experience do you find yourself thinking about most?

options.label: Mine — it was primarily my problem to solve and my stress to carry
My team's — we were all caught up in it together
A specific colleague who seemed to have it harder than me
The customer or person our work ultimately serves

nodes.comment: Route based on axis3 signal accumulated from A3_OPEN

nodes.text: Staying focused on your own experience makes sense — some days demand it. Did you notice anyone around you today who might have been struggling?

options.label: Yes — I noticed, but I didn't have the bandwidth to engage
Yes — I checked in with them, even briefly
Not really — I was genuinely heads-down in my own work
I noticed something felt off in the room, but I'm not sure what

nodes.text: You held others in mind today. What made you tune into them rather than just your own workload?

options.label: It's how I naturally operate — I read the room without trying
Something in their behavior made it impossible not to notice
We're so interconnected that ignoring others doesn't really work
I'm not sure I actually helped — I'm still processing whether I did enough

nodes.comment: Route to deeper Axis 3 question based on accumulated signals

nodes.text: You spent most of today inside your own experience. If you could replay one moment — is there anyone who needed something from you that you might have missed?

options.label: Yes — someone reached out and I didn't have the space to really be there
Maybe — but I genuinely don't know if they needed me specifically
No — I think I handled my responsibilities well enough
Yes — and I want to make a point of checking in tomorrow

nodes.text: You held others in the frame today. When you carry both your own load and awareness of others — does that outward orientation sustain you or cost you?

options.label: It sustains me — their meaning becomes part of mine
It grounds me — my own problems feel smaller in context
It costs me — I end up carrying weight that isn't mine to carry
Both — it depends on the day and the person

nodes.comment: Route to Axis 3 reflection based on final accumulated signals

nodes.text:
Today was mostly yours to carry — your work, your frame, your stress.

That's not wrong. Some days ask for all of you.

But here's a question to sit with tonight: who else was quietly changed by how your day went? You don't have to answer it now. Just notice whether it lands.

Today, you held others in the frame — your team, a colleague, the person your work ultimately serves.

That's not selflessness. It's a wider lens. And a wider lens tends to find meaning where a narrower one finds only exhaustion.

Whatever else today was — you weren't in it alone, and you made sure others weren't either.

You moved between self and others today — sometimes zoomed in tight, sometimes wide enough to include the people around you.

That oscillation is honest. The question worth carrying: when you were most zoomed out, what did it feel like? That feeling is a compass.

Rest well.

Same time tomorrow.
